prompt: A pre-planned one-sided test reports a p-value of 0.03 for an increase. What does it say under its assumed sampling model?

options.text: There is a 3% probability the null is true.
options.explanation: This reverses the conditional and needs a Bayesian model to assess.

options.text: The variant increases the metric by 3%.
options.explanation: Effect size is distinct from a p-value.

options.text: The variant is useful with probability 97%.
options.explanation: Neither posterior truth nor practical value follows from that subtraction.

options.text: Under no effect, a statistic at least this extreme in the planned direction has probability 3%.
options.explanation: The p-value conditions on the null model.

workedExample: Keep the assumption at the start of the sentence: if there were no effect and the sampling model held. Then consider results at least as extreme in the planned direction. Do not invert this into a probability of the hypothesis.

prompt: A planned two-sided A/B test reports a p-value of 0.058 against a pre-specified 0.05 threshold. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Keep collecting until the ordinary p-value drops below 0.05.
options.explanation: That changes the stopping rule and can invalidate fixed-sample error control.

options.text: The observed relative lift alone establishes significance.
options.explanation: Significance depends on uncertainty as well as the observed difference.

options.text: The test has not met its rejection rule; this is not proof of no effect.
options.explanation: Sampling uncertainty may leave a real effect unresolved.

options.text: The two variants are proven identical.
options.explanation: Failure to reject does not establish equivalence.

workedExample: Compare the reported result to the planned rule. Then report effect size and uncertainty without turning an inconclusive test into a proof. A new or sequential analysis needs an appropriate pre-specified design.
